questions.q: What kind of a king was Manasseh for fifty-five years?
questions.a: He did evil things in the sight of Yahweh, rebuilt idols that Hezekiah had torn down, and worshiped the stars of heaven.

questions.q: What did he do to provoke God to anger?
questions.a: Manasseh offered his children as burnt offerings, performed sorcery, and consulted with those that talked with the dead.

questions.q: What did Manasseh do to lead the people of Judah and Jerusalem to do evil?
questions.a: He broke the commandments by placing the carved figure in the house of God.

questions.q: What happened to Manasseh when Yahweh spoke to him and the people?
questions.a: Because they paid no attention, Yahweh had the army of the king of Assyria put Manasseh in chains and take him to Babylon.

questions.q: What did Manasseh do so that God would bring him back to Jerusalem?
questions.a: He humbled himself, prayed, and begged God.

questions.q: After Manasseh prayed, what action did he take to show his remorse?
questions.a: He built a high wall around Judah and took away foreign gods, the idol that he had placed in God’s house, and all the altars he had built.

questions.q: To whom did the people offer sacrifices at the shrines?
questions.a: They offered sacrifices only to Yahweh at the shrines.

questions.q: How were Manasseh’s prayers and important matters preserved?
questions.a: Manasseh’s important matters, prayers, and words of the seers are recorded with the deeds of the kings of Israel.

questions.q: What kind of king was Amon during his two-year reign?
questions.a: He was more evil than his father, he worshiped carved figures, and he did not humble himself before Yahweh.

questions.q: After King Amon’s servants killed him, what did the people of the land do to those who killed him?
questions.a: The people of the land killed all the servants who put Amon to death.

commentary.text: Verses 1–20 We have seen Manasseh's wickedness; here we have his repentance, and a memorable instance it is of the riches of God's pardoning mercy, and the power of his renewing grace. Deprived of his liberty, separated from his evil counsellors and companions, without any prospect but of ending his days in a wretched prison, Manasseh thought upon what had passed; he began to cry for mercy and deliverance. He confessed his sins, condemned himself, was humbled before God, loathing himself as a monster of impiety and wickedness. Yet he hoped to be pardoned through the abundant mercy of the Lord. Then Manasseh knew that Jehovah was God, able to deliver. He knew him as a God of salvation; he learned to fear, trust in, love, and obey him. From this time he bore a new character, and walked in newness of life. Who can tell what tortures of conscience, what pangs of grief, what fears of wrath, what agonizing remorse he endured, when he looked back on his many years of apostacy and rebellion against God; on his having led thousands into sin and perdition; and on his blood-guiltiness in the persecution of a number of God's children? And who can complain that the way of heaven is blocked up, when he sees such a sinner enter? Say the worst against thyself, here is one as bad who finds the way to repentance. Deny not to thyself that which God hath not denied to thee; it is not thy sin, but thy impenitence, that bars heaven against thee. (2Ch 33:21-25)

Amon's father did ill, but he did worse. Whatever warnings or convictions he had, he never humbled himself. He was soon cut off in his sins, and made a warning for all men not to abuse the example of God's patience and mercy to Manasseh, as an encouragement to continue in sin. May God help us to be honest to ourselves, and to think aright respecting our own character, before death fixes us in an unchangeable state.
